c.tagline: Africa's westernmost tip, where Atlantic surf meets vibrant city life.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis lack working meters; negotiate the fare before departure. Tourist-rate taxis and app-based rides are more predictable.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing and aggressive vendors around Plateau, Sandaga market and the Corniche; caution at night

hood_desc: The historic administrative and business core on the southern peninsula tip, with colonial architecture, government buildings, the Place de l'Indépendance and Dakar's main museums; suits first-time visitors wanting to walk to sights and ferries to Gorée Island.

A quiet, leafy, upscale residential district near embassies and the Corniche, popular with expats and NGO workers; suits travelers wanting a calm, safe base with good restaurants a short taxi from downtown.
Dakar's trendiest coastal strip of restaurants, nightlife and beach clubs facing the Îles de la Madeleine; suits visitors who want a resort-like feel with easy beach and surf access.
A small fishing-village peninsula and popular surf beach right next to the airport road, with a laid-back, bohemian vibe; suits surfers, backpackers and those wanting sunset views over the bay.
A relaxed, artsy residential/beach neighborhood near Yoff beach and the airport, home to many guesthouses and yoga/surf retreats; suits budget travelers and long-stay digital nomads.
lodging: Radisson Blu Hotel Dakar Sea Plaza

water.note: Water is treated but aging pipes create contamination risk; most residents and visitors drink bottled water.

transit.pay: Sunu BRT and TER use contactless smart cards or mobile payment tapped at station gates; Dakar Dem Dikk buses and shared car rapide/Ndiaga Ndiaye minibuses are paid in cash to the conductor onboard.
transit.hours: Buses and BRT run roughly 6:00-22:00; TER operates approximately 5:30-22:30; limited night options rely on taxis or ride-hailing apps.
transit.note: The TER links Dakar to Diamniadio near the airport; the new electric Sunu BRT runs along a dedicated corridor from Petersen (Plateau) to Guédiawaye.

bus: Intercity coaches from Gare Routière Pompiers

transit.m: Shared taxi/car rapide to Diamniadio then onward transport

tip.r: Not obligatory but appreciated; rounding up or 5-10% at restaurants is common for good service.

food.name: Thieboudienne
food.desc: Senegal's national dish: fish stuffed with parsley and garlic, simmered with cassava, carrot and cabbage, the broth then used to cook broken rice red or white.

places.name: Chez Loutcha
places.note: Dakar institution for Cape Verdean and Senegalese cooking; enormous portions at bargain prices, lunch is the moment.

places.name: Keur N'Deye
places.note: Long-established Senegalese dining room decorated with local crafts; the classic sit-down thieboudienne.

places.name: Marche Kermel lunch stalls
places.note: Cooks around the colonial market ladle out thieboudienne from communal bowls at midday for a few hundred francs.

food.name: Yassa poulet
food.desc: Chicken grilled then braised in a mountain of onions slow-cooked with lemon, mustard and chilli until jammy, served over white rice.

places.name: Chez Loutcha
places.note: Yassa arrives like a warming onion soup over two chicken thighs or a whole dorade; portions feed two.

places.name: Keur N'Deye
places.note: Consistently good yassa and a calm room, useful if you want table service and a menu in French.

places.name: La Dagorne
places.note: Well-reviewed by 2025 visitors for very fresh fish and properly spicy Senegalese chicken, with attentive service.

food.name: Mafé
food.desc: Beef or lamb stewed in groundnut paste with tomato and root vegetables until thick and russet - the West African peanut stew at its richest.

places.name: Keur N'Deye
places.note: Reliable mafe alongside thieboudienne and yassa; a good place to try all three over a few visits.

places.name: Chez Loutcha
places.note: Rotating daily specials mean mafe appears on set days - ask which dish is being cooked before you sit.

places.name: Marche Kermel lunch stalls
places.note: Street cooks serve mafe from big pots at lunchtime for a fraction of restaurant prices.

food.name: Dibi
food.desc: Lamb or mutton grilled over wood in a dibiterie, chopped on the block, wrapped in paper with raw onion, mustard and chilli and eaten with your hands.

places.name: Point E dibiteries
places.note: Cluster of grills around Avenue Cheikh Anta Diop that fire up in the evening; busiest after 9pm.

places.name: Ouakam dibiteries
places.note: Neighbourhood grills near the mosque where the meat is chopped to order and served on butcher paper.

places.name: Sandaga market grills
places.note: Rough-and-ready street grills around the market; cheapest dibi in the city, cash only.

food.name: Fataya and accara
food.desc: Fried street snacks: fataya, half-moon pastries of spiced fish or meat with onion sauce, and accara, black-eyed pea fritters served in bread with chilli.

places.name: Marche Kermel
places.note: Vendors around the market fry fataya and accara through the day; eat them hot, standing up.

places.name: Marche Sandaga surrounds
places.note: Street carts frying to order all afternoon, the everyday snack of downtown Dakar.

places.name: Ngor and Yoff beach stalls
places.note: Beachfront fryers serving fataya and accara to swimmers and fishermen at sunset.

food.name: Thiakry
food.desc: Steamed millet couscous pearls stirred into sweetened, soured milk with vanilla and nutmeg - the cool, grainy dessert served after a heavy rice plate.

places.name: Keur N'Deye
places.note: Traditional Senegalese desserts including thiakry and sombi rice pudding after the main course.

places.name: Chez Loutcha
places.note: Thiakry and fruit finish the set lunch; ask for it chilled.

places.name: Marche Kermel
places.note: Sold in plastic cups by market vendors alongside bissap and bouye juices.

food.name: Bissap and bouye
food.desc: Deep-red hibiscus infusion sweetened with mint or vanilla, and bouye - creamy, tart juice pressed from baobab fruit and thinned with milk or water.

places.name: Marche Kermel juice vendors
places.note: Frozen sachets and bottles of bissap, bouye and ditakh sold ice-cold beside the produce stalls.

places.name: Keur N'Deye
places.note: House-made bissap and bouye by the carafe with the food, in a hygienic sit-down setting.

places.name: Ngor beach stalls
places.note: Cool juices sold from cool boxes along the beach and on the boat over to Ile de Ngor.

food.name: Cafe Touba
food.desc: Coffee roasted with djar, the peppery Guinea pepper, then boiled and heavily sweetened - a spiced, faintly medicinal brew tied to the Mouride brotherhood.

places.name: Plateau street vendors
places.note: Men with insulated urns pour cafe Touba into small plastic cups from dawn on almost every downtown corner.

places.name: Marche Sandaga surrounds
places.note: Stalls around the market serve it with bread and butter as a working breakfast.

places.name: Medina neighbourhood cafes
places.note: Tiny local cafes where cafe Touba is the default order; the strongest and sweetest versions in town.

landmarks: African Renaissance Monument
A colossal bronze statue towering over Dakar, depicting a family emerging from a volcano, symbolizing Africa's emergence from centuries of adversity.
Gorée Island (House of Slaves)
A UNESCO World Heritage island whose somber House of Slaves and pink colonial buildings preserve the haunting memory of the transatlantic slave trade.
Cathédrale du Souvenir Africain
Dakar's grand Catholic cathedral, an architectural landmark blending European design with African motifs in the heart of the downtown Plateau district.
Grand Mosque of Dakar
An elegant Moroccan-style mosque with a soaring minaret, standing as one of the city's most recognizable religious and architectural landmarks.
Lake Retba (Lac Rose)
A famous pink-hued salt lake near Dakar, its striking rose color caused by unique algae, drawing photographers from around the world.
Mamelles Lighthouse
A historic lighthouse perched atop volcanic hills near the African Renaissance Monument, offering sweeping views of the Atlantic coastline.
Museum of Black Civilizations
A striking circular modern museum celebrating the art, history, and heritage of Black civilizations across Africa and the diaspora.
Sandaga Market
A sprawling, colorful open-air market in central Dakar bursting with fabrics, spices, and crafts, embodying the city's vibrant commercial energy.
Théodore Monod Museum of African Art (IFAN)
One of West Africa's oldest art museums, housing an extensive collection of traditional masks, sculptures, and artifacts from across the continent.
Presidential Palace (Palais de la République)
The stately colonial-era seat of Senegal's presidency, fronted by manicured gardens and guarded by ceremonial troops in colorful uniforms.

train.note: The Dakar-Bamako (Mali) international train has not carried passengers since 2009 and does not run. Rail from Dakar today is only the modern TER commuter line running east to Diamniadio and Blaise Diagne (AIBD) airport - useful locally, not for long-distance travel.

bus.note: State operator Dakar Dem Dikk runs sub-regional coaches under its 'Afrique Dem Dikk' brand, though individual routes start and pause - check current departures with them directly. The traditional alternative is shared sept-places bush taxis from the Gare des Beaux Maraichers to Banjul, Bamako and other regional cities. Carry visas/ECOWAS documents for the countries you cross.

ferry.note: No international passenger ferries from Dakar. Domestic services only: the short Dakar-Goree Island chaloupe from the port, and the overnight Dakar-Ziguinchor ferry to the Casamance region run by COSAMA (ship 'Aline Sitoe Diatta').

half.name: Goree Island
half.blurb: Historic island reached by ferry, known for colonial architecture and its poignant slave-trade heritage.

half.name: Lac Rose (Lac Retba)
half.blurb: Shallow lake glowing pink from algae, ringed by salt harvesters and rolling sand dunes.

half.name: Ngor Island
half.blurb: Tiny car-free island reached by pirogue, loved for calm beaches and laid-back charm.

half.name: Bandia Reserve
half.blurb: Wildlife reserve where safari drives reveal giraffes, rhinos, zebras, and giant baobab trees.

half.name: Saly
half.blurb: Coastal resort town with sandy beaches, palm-lined shores, and a relaxed seaside atmosphere.

half.name: M'bour
half.blurb: Busy fishing town whose vibrant beach market sees colorful pirogues land the daily catch.
